overview: Vallabhi is a historic name painted across two centuries after the Maitraka line that made it famous. The atlas indexes Vallabhi from 800 to 1000 and repeats one polygon at 800 and 900. Yet the latest securely dated Maitraka ruler is recorded in 766, and scholarship places Maitraka Valabhi roughly before 770. No evidence revives a Vallabhi kingdom in 800. The safest reading is an inherited regional label stretched over Saurashtra and northern Gujarat while Rashtrakuta, Gurjara-Pratihara, local, and then Chaulukya powers overlapped. The polygon contains Vallabhipur, Junagadh, Somnath, Dwarka, Ahmedabad, Patan, and Khambhat, but excludes nearby Bhavnagar; it is a teaching envelope, not a surveyed frontier. Copper-plate grants let us meet landholders, Brahmins, officials, villagers, wells, fields, taxes, ritual gifts, and scribes. They say much less about children, ordinary women, medicine, waste, or toilets, so those gaps stay visible. Earlier Valabhi monasteries remain part of the region's inheritance, not proof that their institutions survived unchanged. A securely dated Sanskrit grant from 808 supplies a writing sample for the era. At 1000 the software repaints the whole footprint as “Rajput Kingdoms.” That is an editorial seam, not Vallabhi's fall.

periods.title: 800 to 808: an inherited name after the Maitrakas
periods.summary: The atlas opens Vallabhi in 800, although the last secure Maitraka date is 766 and archaeological syntheses end the dynasty near 770. Early ninth-century Saurashtra belonged to a competitive western Indian landscape. The opening boundary therefore marks a database phase, not the accession of a new Vallabhi king.

periods.title: 808 to 812: Govinda III and a dated Gujarat charter
periods.summary: Govinda III's Radhanpur copper plates, dated in 808, record a Sanskrit land grant with named officials, a learned Brahmin, village boundaries, settled Brahmins, and forty Mahajanas. The charter gives a firm documentary anchor for the atlas era, while its Rashtrakuta authority contradicts any simple Vallabhi-wide monarchy.

periods.title: 812 to 835: a frontier held through subordinates
periods.summary: A Baroda charter of 812-13 associates Karkaraja with authority in central and southern Gujarat and calls him a barrier against the Gurjaras. That language shows frontier rivalry and delegated rule. It does not turn every place inside the atlas polygon into one stable realm or restore Maitraka Vallabhi.

periods.title: 835 to 871: many charters, no revived Vallabhi dynasty
periods.summary: Rashtrakuta history is reconstructed from Gujarat records at Baroda, Surat, Kavi, Begumra, and Sanjan across these decades. Their dates reveal continuing administration and gifts under changing authorities. The documentary density is valuable, but none supplies a Vallabhi royal sequence matching the atlas label or its oversized outline.

periods.title: 871 to 930: religious gifts and regional power
periods.summary: Inscriptions from Sanjan and Begumra continue the record of elite gifts, while Gurjara-Pratihara power framed much of western India. Copper plates preserve transactions and ideals rather than a complete political map. Local lineages, beneficiaries, villages, and religious institutions remained active beneath the empire-sized labels used by later syntheses.

periods.title: 930 to 949: Cambay, waterworks, and ritual generosity
periods.summary: The 930 Cambay plates belong to Govinda IV's documentary world and praise meritorious works such as shelters, water stations, stepwells, wells, tanks, gardens, and temples. This is evidence for the values expressed by a royal charter, not proof that every listed facility existed at Vallabhi or served everyone equally.

periods.title: 949 to 961: Siyaka grants villages beside the Mahi
periods.summary: Siyaka's Harsola grants of 949 describe two villages, assembled residents and officers, Brahmin recipients, pasture, taxes, shares, royalties, and a named scribe. The records show a working political order in eastern Gujarat. They also demonstrate why the atlas's single Vallabhi color hides several regional histories.

periods.title: 961 to 1000: Chaulukya growth before the map repaint
periods.summary: Architectural history places Mularaja and the early Chaulukyas in the tenth-century succession after smaller post-Maitraka houses around Anhilapataka. Patronage by rulers, merchants, and ministers helped shape a new regional landscape. The atlas waits until 1000 to repaint the footprint, so its label lags behind historical change.

sections.title: The name is older than the map dates

items.text: The live index has exactly one Vallabhi record, marked circa and running from 800 to 1000. Coverage points to two border files, one at 800 and one at 900. Those are firm facts about this atlas, not evidence that a ruler in Vallabhi issued a two-century lease on history.

Both target snapshots decode to the same single polygon: one component, one ring, thirty positions, and identical geometry hashes. Its bounds reach from Saurashtra into northern and central Gujarat. Repetition shows that the atlas reused a shape for convenience; it does not turn that outline into a medieval surveyed border.

Vallabhipur, Talaja, Junagadh, Somnath, Dwarka, Porbandar, Rajkot, Ahmedabad, Patan, Vadnagar, Kheda, and Khambhat test inside the polygon. That is a large and varied region. A useful map can group places, but the grouping must not be mistaken for uniform administration or identity.

Bhavnagar, Vadodara, Bharuch, Surat, Radhanpur, Bhuj, Mount Abu, and Ujjain test outside. The funniest cartographic clue is also serious: nearby Bhavnagar falls outside the Vallabhi shape while faraway Patan lies inside. The polygon is a teaching envelope drawn with a very broad digital paintbrush.

At 800 the polygon shares imported arcs with Hindu States and Gurjara-Pratihara features; at 900 the northern neighbor changes to Sindh while Gurjara-Pratihara remains. Shared arcs tell us how map tiles meet. They do not prove alliances, wars, languages, or customs along a real frontier.

sections.title: Land, fields, and the tax trail

items.text: The 808 Radhanpur charter grants Rattajuna village in the Rastriyana district and names boundary markers on four sides. It addresses officials, settled Brahmins, and forty Mahajanas. The legal detail shows land being defined through known rivers and neighboring villages, while saying little about how cultivators experienced the transfer.

Earlier Maitraka plates from Maliya describe measured plots, a carpenter's plot, stepwells, houses, and named cultivators, with references to sugarcane, cotton, hemp, mango, and mahua. These details illuminate the inheritance of pre-800 Gujarat. They are clues, not a time machine proving identical farms in the tenth century.

Regional economic texts discuss grain shares, agricultural taxes, tolls, customary payments, and labor obligations. Such demands linked rulers and grantees to productive households. The documents mostly record what elites expected to receive, so a neat tax formula should never be mistaken for a complete diary of village work or hardship.

The 949 Harsola grants transfer Kumbharotaka and Sihaka villages with pasture rights, dues, shares, royalties, and gold payments. Residents and officers are summoned to recognize the gifts. This is concrete evidence of claims over revenue, but the charter preserves the grantor's legal voice rather than villagers' consent.

Copper plates survive because metal and institutional memory are stubborn. They disproportionately reveal durable property claims, named beneficiaries, and formal exemptions. Families who weeded, carried water, tended animals, or owed shares seldom speak for themselves. The paperwork is rich evidence, but it comes with an elite-shaped spotlight.

Rashtrakuta history draws on plates from Radhanpur, Baroda, Surat, Kavi, Begumra, Sanjan, Kapadvanj, and Cambay between 808 and 930. The spread shows documents and authority moving across Gujarat's connected places. It does not prove that every stop belonged to one Vallabhi-centered government.

The Cambay plates were preserved at Khambhat, a place inside the atlas polygon, and anchor a royal charter in 930. A findspot can show where a document entered later custody, but it cannot by itself reconstruct a port's entire traffic, market population, or shipping schedule. Archaeology and other records must do that work.

Gurjara-Pratihara rulers operated on an imperial scale during the ninth and tenth centuries, using grants and monumental patronage to display power. Their reach helps explain why the region cannot be read as an isolated Vallabhi survival. Empire names, however, still leave room for local officers, lineages, and negotiated authority.

Regional temples were rebuilt, adapted, and compared through changing architectural styles. Art historians can trace relationships among plans, roofs, carving, and workshops, but style rarely supplies a day-exact political border. A shrine may outlast several rulers, which makes architecture a patient witness and a rather unreliable customs officer.

The polygon includes coastal Dwarka and Somnath, inland Patan, Ahmedabad, and Khambhat, plus many landscapes between them. That geographic span encourages stories about travel and exchange, yet the atlas geometry itself proves none. Routes, markets, and journeys need independent evidence; a colored region is not a medieval bus timetable.

Before 800, Maitraka charters show mostly Shaiva kings granting to Brahmins as well as Buddhist monasteries and other religious beneficiaries. Roughly seventy percent of the studied charters concern Brahman recipients and about a quarter Buddhist monasteries. This mixed patronage is the region's inheritance, not proof of unchanged institutions afterward.

Dudda, a niece of Dhruvasena I and a Buddhist laywoman, founded a monastery at Valabhi in the sixth century. Later grants supported it. Her story makes elite women's religious agency visible, but it belongs centuries before this card's opening and cannot stand in for all women or every monastery in 800.

Earlier Valabhi endowments supplied monasteries with food, beds, clothing, medicine, ritual materials, repairs, villages, fields, wells, tanks, and flower gardens. The list shows how institutions were imagined as material communities, not only prayer halls. Survival of each provision after the Maitrakas must be demonstrated, not assumed.

The 808 Radhanpur recipient is described through Brahmin status, Bharadvaja lineage, Vedic learning, and performance of the five great sacrifices. Those labels reveal the charter's ideal social and ritual credentials. They tell us much less about neighboring devotional practice or people who never received copper-plate introductions.

The 930 Cambay charter praises shelters, water facilities, gardens, and temples among meritorious works. Such lists joined public benefit, royal reputation, and religious merit in a single literary frame. They reveal values expressed by donors, while leaving open who built, maintained, entered, or was excluded from each facility.

Written-language sample, Sanskrit: “तेनेदम् अनिलविद्युच्चाञ्चलम् आलोक्य जीवितम् असारम्.” Transliteration: “tenedaṃ anilavidyuccāñcalam ālokya jīvitaṃ asāraṃ.” Meaning: seeing life as insubstantial and unsteady like wind and lightning. It comes from Govinda III's copper-plate grant dated 808, securely inside this card's era.

The sample is modern Unicode Devanagari with editorial word spacing, not a tracing of the eighth-century letterforms. The published facsimile preserves the actual Brahmi-derived script. The plates were found at Radhanpur, outside this atlas polygon, so they represent the era's regional documentary culture rather than a voice from Vallabhi city.

Copper plates were legal objects built for endurance: genealogy and praise led into the gift, boundaries, beneficiaries, conditions, date, and authentication. They are wonderfully informative land deeds, not medieval family group chats. Their formal Sanskrit makes power audible while ordinary conversation remains almost entirely offstage.

The Harsola grants name Kayastha Gunadhara as writer and preserve Siyaka's sign manual, making the production chain partly visible. Someone composed, wrote, checked, handled, and safeguarded these texts. Literacy was skilled work embedded in administration; the named scribe should not be mistaken for a count of all literate people.

Dated inscriptions are precious because they pin an event, donor, place, and formula to a chronological peg. The Gujarat register includes many such pegs from 808 onward. Large spaces remain between them, and a run of copper plates cannot substitute for lost letters, oral teaching, account books, or household notes.

The 949 Harsola records grant villages to a Nagar Brahmin father and son from Anandapura. That relationship proves one documented family link and shows status carried through learned lineage. It does not establish the typical household, marriage age, inheritance practice, or emotional life of farming, herding, craft, or service families.

Dudda's earlier monastery foundation records an elite woman acting as a donor in her own name. Her royal kinship helped make that action legible to the charter tradition. She widens the story beyond kings, but her exceptional visibility warns against treating palace-connected patronage as ordinary women's daily experience.

Maitraka Buddhist establishments could be founded by noblewomen, officials, monks, traders, and other private donors. The variety shows that religious patronage reached beyond the throne, although wealth and access still shaped whose gifts reached metal. The evidence is pre-800 background and must not be stretched into an unchanged later social map.

Charters sort people by ruler, officer, Brahmin learning, lineage, resident, cultivator, and beneficiary. These categories organized duties and privilege on the page. Social reality was surely more tangled: neighbors cooperated, disputed, married, moved, and worked across categories, but their relationships rarely survive in the legal formulas available here.

The Radhanpur order addresses officials, resident Brahmins, and forty Mahajanas, a ranked public assembled around a grant. No wife, daughter, household servant, or laborer speaks directly. Family and social life certainly existed; the responsible card distinguishes that obvious truth from details the surviving document never records.

The 808 recipient is called a student of three Vedas and specifically connected with the Taittiriya tradition. That proves advanced learned identity, not a universal school system. Training probably required teachers, memorization, recitation, and long practice, but the charter does not describe classrooms, lesson times, fees, or children's first day.

Earlier Valabhi monasteries, grants, and manuscript culture helped later writers remember the city as a center of learning. Archaeological tablets and institutional endowments support a literate religious environment before 800. They do not certify that a famous university continued through every year of the atlas's 800 to 1000 interval.

No reviewed source securely describes a child's ordinary day in ninth- or tenth-century Vallabhi: no toy inventory tied to this label, no school roll, no bedtime story, and no child's letter. Children should remain in the card as a visible evidence gap rather than being filled with charming but invented routines.

Farming, writing, temple building, metalwork, and administration all required learned skills. Apprenticeship within households or specialist groups is a reasonable historical possibility, but these sources do not date or describe it for children here. The safest fun fact is methodological: grown-up paperwork is surprisingly good at hiding young people.

Education was unequal. A charter celebrates one learned Brahmin because his credentials mattered to the gift; it says nothing comparable about girls, cultivators' children, herders, artisans, or servants. Absence from the plate is not absence from intelligence or teaching. It is evidence about what the record-makers valued enough to engrave.

Pre-800 land records name sugarcane, cotton, hemp, mango, and mahua, alongside fields, houses, cattle spaces, forests, and mines. The plants suggest food, fiber, oil, drink, and craft possibilities in earlier Gujarat. They cannot be turned into a guaranteed Vallabhi dinner menu or wardrobe for 900.

Surface finds around ancient Vala include terracotta Buddhist creed tablets, plaques, stone fragments, and traces of monasteries, while standing buildings are sparse. Small fired-clay objects can outlast lunch, laundry, and gossip by centuries. Archaeology therefore preserves durable fragments of daily life while the soft, edible, and spoken parts disappear.

Taxes and grants depended on people plowing, watering, tending cattle, carrying produce, and maintaining productive land. The economic sources document claims on that labor more clearly than workers' own choices. Daily work was the engine beneath royal generosity, even when the charter gives the donor the best seat in the sentence.

Regional temple sculpture and architecture required designers, quarry workers, carvers, transporters, masons, finishers, donors, and ritual specialists. The surviving monuments display coordinated expertise, though they rarely preserve a complete payroll. A carved stone is an achievement shared by many hands, even when an inscription spotlights only a patron.

The Harsola grants mention pasture and rights over village revenues, placing animals and cultivated land inside the fiscal picture. They do not list family recipes, loom patterns, garment cuts, or meal schedules. Clothing and food were essential, but this exact period's reviewed records offer fewer safe details than their official language might suggest.

The 930 Cambay charter lists shelters, water stations, stepwells, wells, tanks, gardens, and temples as meritorious works. The list shows that access to water and maintained public facilities carried social and religious value. It does not prove a standardized municipal network or equal access across the atlas polygon.

A 605 Maitraka grant supported a monastery with a village, fields, irrigation cisterns, wells, and flower gardens. This earlier example shows how water infrastructure could be endowed around Valabhi. Because it predates the card by almost two centuries, it is inheritance evidence, not a maintenance certificate valid in 800.

Earlier Valabhi monastic grants explicitly include medicine among provisions for religious residents. That proves organized medical support in a particular institutional setting before 800. The reviewed 800 to 1000 sources do not identify a Vallabhi physician, clinic, treatment manual, vaccination, or universal care system, so the later picture remains open.

No reviewed source securely identifies a toilet, latrine, sewer, household drain, or waste-collection rule for Vallabhi between 800 and 1000. Wells and tanks are not toilets, and silence is not proof that people ignored hygiene. It means we lack the archaeological or textual plumbing inspection certificate needed for specifics.

Water facilities require cleaning, repair, rules, and labor, but a merit list does not describe those routines. People had to manage mud, refuse, animals, and contaminated water somehow; the exact arrangements are undocumented here. Responsible history can explain the practical problem without inventing a tidy sewer plan beneath a colorful polygon.

sections.title: 1000 is a repaint, not a fall

items.text: The strongest chronological correction is simple: 766 is the latest secure date for a Maitraka dynast, decades before this card begins. Later royal sequences have been reconstructed too confidently from thin evidence. Calling the 800 to 1000 feature Vallabhi is therefore an atlas convention, not proof of a hidden two-century dynasty.

The 800 and 900 snapshots contain the same Vallabhi geometry, down to its decoded hash. Political history did not freeze for a hundred years; the source data did. The unchanged polygon should be read as a coarse editorial holding shape while inscriptions document multiple rulers, offices, and regional transitions.

At 1000 every tested place formerly inside Vallabhi is assigned to a generic Rajput Kingdoms feature. The target simply disappears, with no separate successor list or dated conquest encoded. The seam records a change in the map's labeling system, not a synchronized collapse from Dwarka to Patan and Khambhat.

By the tenth century, smaller post-Maitraka houses and the rising Chaulukyas were reshaping Gujarat. Mularaja's rule belongs before or around the atlas endpoint, and merchants and ministers joined rulers as patrons. Historical transition was already underway while the old Vallabhi label remained on screen.

The 1100 control map assigns most probes to the Solanki feature, confirming another broad editorial phase after 1000. Continuity belongs to places and communities, not to the Vallabhi polygon. Vallabhipur, farms, shrines, roads, waterworks, and families did not blink out when the software reached its next color.

ending.text: The atlas ends Vallabhi at 1000 by repainting its entire tested footprint as “Rajput Kingdoms,” then mostly as “Solankis” by 1100. No reviewed source records a Vallabhi state falling in 1000, and the Maitraka dynasty had ended long before 800. Gujarat's tenth-century political transition toward Chaulukya power was already underway. Vallabhipur and the region's people, farms, shrines, and documentary traditions continued through changing authorities. The database therefore keeps fell null and names no single successor: 1000 is an editorial seam, not a conquest date.
